title: Vasopressors, inotropes & vasodilators
summary: Circulatory support agents with standard dilutions.

sections.title: Key points
items: Give peripheral vasopressor only as a bridge through a large, well-sited cannula with frequent site checks under local policy; move to central access as soon as it is safe.
Titrate to a mean arterial pressure target set for the patient, not to a fixed rate, and reassess volume state and cardiac output before adding a second agent.
Double-strength bags exist for fluid-restricted patients — always confirm the concentration on the syringe label against the pump library before handover.
Vasodilator infusions need continuous arterial pressure monitoring; stop rather than titrate down when pressure falls abruptly.

title: Sedation & anaesthesia
summary: Induction agents, volatiles, sedative infusions and their antagonists.

sections.title: Key points
items: Set a sedation target (for example RASS −1 to 0) and assess it at least once a nursing shift; daily interruption shortens ventilation where it is safe.
Watch cumulative propofol dose, triglycerides and lactate for propofol-related infusion syndrome in prolonged high-dose use.

Sedative effects may be prolonged by drug accumulation and organ impairment. Unexpected failure to wake requires prompt assessment for drug effects and other causes, including hypoxia, metabolic disturbance and neurological pathology; do not assume accumulation is the explanation.
Sedation is not analgesia: treat pain first, then add sedation only if a target is still unmet.

title: Opioids & analgesia
summary: Opioids, NSAIDs and adjuncts, with equivalence and safety limits.

sections.title: Key points
items: Use multimodal analgesia — paracetamol plus an NSAID where safe reduces opioid need and opioid-related adverse effects.

Morphine and its active metabolites can accumulate in renal impairment. Choose the opioid and adjust the dose and/or lengthen the dosing interval using renal guidance; oxycodone also requires caution and dose adjustment. Monitor closely for sedation and respiratory depression.
Convert between opioids using published equivalence, then reduce by 25–50% for incomplete cross-tolerance and re-titrate.
After more than a week of opioid or alpha-2 agonist infusion, plan a taper — abrupt discontinuation causes agitation, tachycardia and diarrhoea.

title: Neuromuscular blockers & reversal
summary: Depolarising and non-depolarising blockers with reversal agents.

sections.title: Key points
items: Never give a neuromuscular blocker without a secured or immediately securable airway and a working means of ventilation.
Monitor depth with a nerve stimulator whenever a blocker is infused; aim for a documented train-of-four target.
Ensure adequate sedation and analgesia before paralysis — paralysis hides awareness and pain.
Suxamethonium is contraindicated where hyperkalaemia is likely (burns beyond 24 hours, prolonged immobility, denervation, established critical illness).

title: Local anaesthetics & toxicity rescue
summary: Dose limits, adjuncts and lipid emulsion rescue.

sections.title: Key points
items: Check the drug-specific maximum dose in the product information and local guidance before drawing up, and state it during the block checklist.
Aspirate and inject incrementally with continuous verbal contact; early signs are perioral tingling, tinnitus, metallic taste and agitation.

For suspected severe local anaesthetic systemic toxicity, stop local anaesthetic administration, summon help, support oxygenation and ventilation, and follow the current Association of Anaesthetists emergency algorithm. Its initial 20% lipid regimen is 1.5 mL/kg IV over 2–3 minutes followed by 15 mL/kg/h; follow the algorithm for repeat doses and escalation, without exceeding a cumulative 12 mL/kg.
Continue resuscitation well beyond the usual duration — recovery after bupivacaine arrest can take over an hour.

title: Antiarrhythmics & rate control
summary: Rhythm and rate control agents, including beta-blockade.

sections.title: Key points
items: Correct potassium, magnesium, hypoxia, pain and hypovolaemia before escalating antiarrhythmic drugs — new atrial fibrillation in critical illness is usually secondary.
In an unstable tachyarrhythmia, synchronised cardioversion comes before any drug.

For a regular narrow-complex tachyarrhythmia without life-threatening features, follow the current RCUK algorithm: vagal manoeuvres, then adenosine if there is no pre-excitation, using 6 mg, 12 mg and 18 mg rapid IV boluses if preceding doses are unsuccessful, with continuous ECG monitoring and appropriate resuscitation facilities. This is guideline dosing and may differ from the product licence; check contraindications and patient-specific dose adjustments.
Amiodarone by peripheral vein causes phlebitis — use central access for anything beyond a single loading dose.

title: Anticoagulation, antiplatelets & reversal
summary: Thromboprophylaxis, treatment doses, thrombolysis and reversal agents.

sections.title: Key points
items: Confirm the indication and the target (prophylaxis versus treatment) before prescribing — the doses differ several-fold.
Low molecular weight heparin needs dose reduction and, in some settings, anti-Xa monitoring in renal impairment and extremes of weight.
Know the reversal pathway for every agent you start: protamine, vitamin K with prothrombin complex, idarucizumab or andexanet.
Record the last dose time before any neuraxial procedure and apply the published interval — this is the commonest avoidable harm.

title: Fluids, blood products & electrolytes
summary: Crystalloids, colloids, blood components, diuretics and electrolyte replacement.

sections.title: Key points
items: Prescribe fluid as a named indication (resuscitation, replacement or maintenance) with a volume and a rate, then reassess after each bolus.
Balanced crystalloid is the default resuscitation fluid; large-volume 0.9% sodium chloride causes hyperchloraemic acidosis.
Give concentrated potassium only by a monitored central route at an agreed maximum rate; correct magnesium at the same time.
Blood components need a documented threshold or bleeding indication, positive patient identification and observation for the first 15 minutes.

title: Antimicrobials & antifungals
summary: Antibacterials, antifungals and antivirals with level monitoring where needed.

sections.title: Key points
items: Take appropriate microbiological samples before antibiotics where this will not delay urgent treatment. For adults at high risk of severe illness or death from suspected sepsis, give IV antibiotics within 1 hour under NICE NG253. Moderate- and low-risk presentations require the guideline's risk-stratified assessment and treatment timings.
Dose by mechanism — time-dependent agents need frequent or extended infusions, concentration-dependent agents need adequate peak doses.
Loading and maintenance dose changes in renal impairment are drug-specific — check the product information and local antimicrobial guidance for each agent.
Review at 48–72 hours against culture results and set a stop or step-down date at the time of prescribing.

title: Respiratory drugs
summary: Bronchodilators, methylxanthines and respiratory stimulants.

sections.title: Key points
items: Give nebulised or inhaled bronchodilator by the route that reaches the airway — in ventilated patients use an in-circuit device and check the dose reaching the patient.
Repeated beta-2 agonist causes tachycardia, tremor, hypokalaemia and lactataemia; recheck potassium after back-to-back nebulisers.
Magnesium sulfate is an adjunct in severe acute asthma, not a first-line bronchodilator.
Aminophylline and theophylline have a narrow therapeutic window and need blood level monitoring.

title: Antiemetics & gastrointestinal drugs
summary: Antiemetics, acid suppression, prokinetics and splanchnic agents.

sections.title: Key points
items: Combine antiemetics from different receptor classes rather than repeating the same class for breakthrough nausea.
Check the QT interval and other QT-prolonging drugs before repeated ondansetron, droperidol or metoclopramide.

Use stress-ulcer prophylaxis for critically ill adults with relevant bleeding risk factors. Enteral feeding alone is not a reason to stop it while those risk factors persist. Review daily and discontinue when the critical illness or relevant risk factors resolve, unless another indication remains.
Prokinetics are a short trial for feed intolerance — review at 48 hours and stop if ineffective.

Guideline for the prevention of upper gastrointestinal bleeding in critically ill adults — SCCM / ASHP

title: Endocrine & metabolic drugs
summary: Insulin, corticosteroids and other hormonal agents.

sections.title: Key points
items: Run variable-rate insulin against an agreed glucose target with hourly monitoring; avoid tight control, which causes hypoglycaemia.
Never stop long-acting basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, even when the patient is nil by mouth.

Assess the risk of adrenal insufficiency in patients receiving or recently exposed to glucocorticoids. Those with adrenal insufficiency or clinically significant adrenal suppression need an agreed perioperative steroid plan, in addition to their usual treatment; requirements depend on exposure and surgical stress.
Check the steroid indication and duration — low-dose hydrocortisone in septic shock is a defined course, not an open-ended prescription.

title: Anticonvulsants & neurological drugs
summary: Status epilepticus and maintenance anticonvulsants, several needing blood levels.

sections.title: Key points
items: In status epilepticus give a benzodiazepine first, twice at most, then a second-line agent — levetiracetam, phenytoin or sodium valproate — and plan anaesthesia if seizures continue.
Phenytoin needs a rate limit, cardiac monitoring during loading and level monitoring corrected for albumin.
Look for and treat the cause alongside the drug: glucose, sodium, calcium, eclampsia, drug withdrawal, infection and structural lesions.
Continue established anticonvulsants through critical illness, converting to an equivalent parenteral dose where one exists.

title: Antidotes & emergency drugs
summary: Antidotes, anticholinergics and rescue agents kept for emergencies.

sections.title: Key points
items: Know where the malignant hyperthermia, cyanide and lipid emulsion boxes are kept and who reconstitutes them — dantrolene needs several pairs of hands.
Give the antidote alongside supportive care, never instead of it: airway, oxygen, circulation and decontamination come first.
Contact the national poisons service early for any unfamiliar or mixed overdose.
Check antidote stock and expiry as part of the routine emergency equipment check.

title: Obstetric drugs
summary: Uterotonics and prostaglandins for postpartum haemorrhage.

sections.title: Key points
items: Escalate through the uterotonic ladder while treating the other causes of postpartum haemorrhage — tone, tissue, trauma and thrombin.
Oxytocin bolus causes vasodilatation and tachycardia: give slowly, and follow with an infusion rather than repeated boluses.
Ergometrine is contraindicated in hypertension and pre-eclampsia.

Carboprost can cause bronchospasm. Active pulmonary disease is contraindicated in the Hemabate SmPC; a history of asthma requires careful benefit–risk assessment and senior obstetric/anaesthetic guidance. Follow local restrictions.

Postpartum haemorrhage (separate from the trauma regimen): for clinically diagnosed PPH, give tranexamic acid 1 g IV over 10 minutes as soon as possible and within 3 hours of birth, alongside standard haemorrhage care. A second 1 g dose may be given if bleeding continues after 30 minutes or restarts within 24 hours.

title: Immunosuppressants
summary: Transplant immunosuppression; several agents need blood level monitoring.

sections.title: Key points
items: Never omit or delay transplant immunosuppression without transplant team advice — rejection risk outweighs most perioperative concerns.
Calcineurin inhibitors interact heavily through CYP3A4: check every new antifungal, macrolide and antiepileptic against them.
Take trough levels immediately before the dose and record the exact sampling and dosing times on the request.
Watch renal function, magnesium, potassium, glucose and blood pressure while levels are being adjusted.

title: Infusions — Sedation and analgesia
summary: Analgesia first, then sedative titrated to a target score (e.g. RASS 0 to −2) with daily review. Infusion rates below are adult starting points — obesity, age and organ failure all change requirements.

sections.title: Propofol 1%
sections.text: For adult ICU sedation use the lowest effective rate within the product's recommended range, generally 0.3–4 mg/kg/h. Review continuously and monitor for propofol infusion syndrome (lactic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis, hypertriglyceridaemia); risk increases with higher doses and prolonged use, especially above 4 mg/kg/h for more than 48 hours. Suspected toxicity requires prompt action, not waiting until 48 hours. Lipid load ~1.1 kcal/mL.

rows.label: Draw up
rows.value: 500 mg (25 mL of 2%) made up to 50 mL (10 mg/mL)

sections.text: Opioid-sparing intravenous lidocaine. Maximum 1.5 mg/kg/h using ideal body weight, with an absolute maximum of 120 mg/h; do not use in patients below 40 kg under the cited consensus. Limit to 24 hours with review. If a loading dose is used, no more than 1.5 mg/kg over 10 minutes. Follow local governance, dedicated infusion and monitoring requirements. Avoid overlapping other local anaesthetic interventions; the consensus specifies a 4-hour interval around nerve blocks. Stop if there are any signs of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity; lipid emulsion must be available.

rows.label: Draw up
rows.value: Major trauma: 1 g IV over 10 minutes, then 1 g over 8 hours (prepared per local protocol, e.g. 1 g made up to 50 mL = 20 mg/mL)

sections.text: TRAUMA regimen (not postpartum haemorrhage — see the Obstetric topic for that regimen). Current UK guideline: NICE NG39 recommends IV tranexamic acid as soon as possible in major trauma with active or suspected active bleeding, and not more than 3 hours after injury unless there is evidence of hyperfibrinolysis. Dosing regimen: 1 g over 10 minutes then 1 g over 8 hours (fixed 125 mg/h maintenance), as used in the CRASH-2 randomised trial — a trial regimen, not itself a guideline; follow your local major-haemorrhage protocol. Adjust in renal impairment per the product information and local protocol. Never give by the intrathecal or epidural route — accidental spinal administration is fatal.

title: Adult anaesthetic premedication
summary: For adults aged 18 years and over. Premedication is given before induction to reduce anxiety and smooth the induction itself. It is used selectively — most fit adults need none. Doses below summarise common UK practice; several uses are off-label and should follow local policy. Clinical verification of this page is in progress.

sections.title: General principles
items: Choose the agent to match the goal: anxiolysis and amnesia (midazolam) versus rousable sedation with analgesic sparing (clonidine, dexmedetomidine).

Anyone given a sedative premed needs documented monitoring (SpO₂, respiratory rate, level of consciousness) and a named person responsible until handover to the anaesthetic team. Flumazenil must be immediately available when midazolam is used.
Reduce doses in older and frail adults, obstructive sleep apnoea, and significant cardiac, respiratory, hepatic or renal impairment.
Avoid routine sedative premedication where a rapid wake-up is needed, in airway obstruction risk, and in raised intracranial pressure.
In pregnancy and breastfeeding, check each drug's product information and local obstetric guidance before use.

sources.title: Guidelines for the Provision of Anaesthesia Services (GPAS) — Royal College of Anaesthetists

sections.title: Midazolam — oral
sections.text: Benzodiazepine giving anxiolysis and anterograde amnesia. Onset 15–30 minutes.
items: Paradoxical agitation or disinhibition can occur — observe, do not re-dose automatically.
Caution with other CNS depressants (opioids, antihistamines); recovery may be delayed after day-case surgery.

rows.label: Adult — oral
rows.value: 7.5–15 mg (oral solution/tablet); halve in older or frail adults. Timing: 30–60 min before induction

sections.title: Clonidine — oral
sections.text: Alpha-2 agonist used off-label for sedative premedication. Bradycardia, hypotension and excessive sedation are important risks; appropriate airway and respiratory monitoring remain necessary. Slower onset than midazolam, so it suits planned rather than last-minute premedication. Premedication use is off-label and no claim-level source is held here for a dose or timing, so none is given: use an individualised plan under an agreed local protocol.
items: Avoid or reduce the dose in conduction disease, hypovolaemia or with other negative chronotropes.
Reduces volatile and opioid requirements; plan induction and analgesia doses accordingly.
Longer sedation than midazolam — allow for a slower recovery in day-case pathways.

sections.title: Dexmedetomidine — intranasal
sections.text: Off-label specialist use only, under an agreed local protocol. The IV product SmPC does not support intranasal use, so this app gives no standard intranasal dose or preparation. Bradycardia and hypotension are important adverse effects; respiratory depression, airway obstruction and apnoea can also occur, so cardiac and respiratory monitoring are required.
items: Avoid in heart block, severe ventricular dysfunction and hypovolaemia, and use caution with other rate-slowing drugs.
Context only: one adult randomised trial used 1 microgram/kg given 45–60 minutes before surgery. This is a trial regimen, not a general UK recommendation.

sections.title: Gabapentinoids — gabapentin and pregabalin
sections.text: Gabapentinoids are not a routine premedication choice. Potential analgesic benefit must be weighed against sedation, dizziness and respiratory depression; evidence does not establish a single optimal perioperative dose or timing. Use only an individualised plan under local guidance; prevention of chronic postsurgical pain is not established.
items: Assess whether use is appropriate in older or frail adults, sleep apnoea and respiratory disease. Adjust gabapentin or pregabalin using the medicine-specific renal-function dosing table and monitor sedation and breathing; a universal 50% dose reduction is not appropriate.
Additive sedation and respiratory depression with opioids; severe respiratory depression has also been reported without opioids.

sections.title: Pre-emptive simple analgesia
sections.text: Oral paracetamol and an NSAID given with the pre-operative sip of water are part of most multimodal and enhanced recovery pathways.
items: Count all oral, IV and combination-product paracetamol doses, and record the pre-operative dose clearly so the daily maximum is not exceeded.

Avoid NSAIDs in renal impairment, active peptic ulceration, significant bleeding risk, severe asthma with known sensitivity and some bowel and bone-graft surgery. Check product information for use in pregnancy and breastfeeding.

sections.title: Antiemetic prophylaxis
sections.text: Risk-scored prophylaxis (Apfel) is usually given at induction rather than as a true premed, but oral dosing on the ward is an option in high-risk patients and in those with severe previous post-operative nausea and vomiting.
items: Ondansetron prolongs the QT interval — avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs and correct electrolytes.
Warn the patient that dexamethasone commonly causes a brief perineal burning sensation if given awake, and check the glucose in diabetes.

sections.text: Can be applied on the ward to potential cannulation sites before intravenous induction.
items: EMLA causes vasoconstriction and can make veins harder to see; tetracaine causes vasodilatation and mild erythema, which usually helps.
Do not apply to broken skin, mucous membranes or the eye, and remove tetracaine on time to avoid blistering.
